title: How many cups to break even?
hook: The stand costs $300 a day. Sell $300 of lemonade and you are even. Right?

knows: a business has costs that do not depend on sales (rent, a licence)
doesNotKnow: that fixed costs are repaid one unit at a time by what each sale leaves after its own cost

misconception: I break even when I have sold as much as I spent.
objective: The learner can compute break-even as the fixed cost divided by what each unit leaves after its own cost, and explain why revenue at break-even is more than the fixed cost.

claims.text: With $300 a day of fixed cost, $1 to make each cup and a $3 price, each cup leaves $2 and the stand breaks even at 150 cups.
At $4 a cup the stand breaks even at 100 cups; at $2, at 300 cups.
The 150 cups bring in $450: $150 pays for the cups themselves and $300 for the day.
Break-even is the fixed cost divided by what each unit leaves after its own cost.
claims.source: Break-even quantity = fixed cost / (price − variable cost per unit), the contribution-margin formula in introductory managerial accounting (e.g. Garrison, Noreen & Brewer, Managerial Accounting, cost-volume-profit chapter).

claims.text: The lesson is a model: the same price and cost for every cup, and every cup made is sold.
claims.source: Stage chip 'Model: steady price, $1 a cup to make'; reveal's last line.

recall.question: A food truck pays $600 a day to operate. Each taco costs $2 to make and sells for $5. How many tacos does it need to sell to break even?
recall.why: Each taco leaves $5 − $2 = $3 toward the day's $600, so 600 / 3 = 200 tacos.
